explain.say: As the piston rises, it leaves low pressure below it. The air pressing on the water underground pushes water up the pipe, through the lower valve, into the cylinder.

faq.q: What do the valves in a hand pump do?
faq.a: They are one-way valves. The lower one lets water into the cylinder but not back down the pipe, and the one in the piston lets water move up past the piston but not back down.
asks: Why do pumps need one-way valves?

faq.q: Why does a hand pump give water in spurts?
faq.a: Water only rises on the up stroke of the piston, so the flow comes in pulses, one per pump of the handle.
asks: Why does the water come out in gushes?

faq.q: How deep can a hand pump suck water?
faq.a: A suction pump is really letting air pressure push the water up, and air pressure can hold up at most about 10 metres of water. In practice it works to about 7 metres; deeper wells need a pump down in the water.
asks: Why can a pump not suck water from very deep?

faq.q: Does the pump really suck the water?
faq.a: Not exactly. The piston lowers the pressure above the water, and the higher air pressure on the water outside pushes it up the pipe.
asks: What pushes water up a suction pump?

faq.q: Why do you sometimes have to pour water in first?
faq.a: If the valves are dry, they leak air and cannot hold low pressure. Pouring in water seals them so the pump can start lifting, which is called priming.
asks: Why do you prime a hand pump?

facts: Air pressure can support a column of water only about 10 metres tall, which limits suction pumps.
Piston pumps use one-way valves so water can only move in one direction.
